questions.question: A hole is drilled in a metal sheet. At $27^{\circ}\text{C}$, the diameter of hole is $5\text{ cm}$. When the sheet is heated to $177^{\circ}\text{C}$, the change in the diameter of hole is $d \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm}$. The value of $d$ will be ______ if coefficient of linear expansion of the metal is $1.6 \times 10^{-5} / {^{\circ}\text{C}}$.
questions.explanation: The change in diameter ($\Delta D$) due to linear expansion is given by the formula: $\Delta$ D = D $\alpha \Delta$ T Given values are: • Initial diameter $D = 5\text{ cm}$ • Coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha = 1.6 \times 10^{-5} / {^{\circ}\text{C}}$ • Initial temperature $T_1 = 27^{\circ}\text{C}$ • Final temperature $T_2 = 177^{\circ}\text{C}$ First, calculate the change in temperature $\Delta T$: $\Delta$ T = $T_2 - T_1 = 177^{$\circ$} \text{C} - 27^{$\circ$} \text{C} = 150^{$\circ$} \text{C}$ Now, substitute the values into the expansion formula: $\Delta$ D = 5 \times 1.6 \times $10^{-5}$ \times (177 - 27) $\Delta$ D = 5 \times 1.6 \times $10^{-5}$ \times 150 $\Delta$ D = 8 \times $10^{-5}$ \times 150 $\Delta$ D = 1200 \times $10^{-5} \Delta$ D = 12 \times $10^{-3} \text{ cm}$ The problem states that the change in diameter is $d \times 10^{-3}\text{ cm}$. Comparing this with our calculated value: d \times $10^{-3} \text{ cm}$ = 12 \times $10^{-3} \text{ cm}$ Therefore, the value of $d$ is: d = 12

questions.question: The heat extracted out of x gram of water initially at $50^{\circ}C$ to cool it down to $0^{\circ}C$ is sufficient to evaporate $(1000 – x)$ gram of water also initially at $50^{\circ}C$. The value of x (closest integer) is _____. (Take latent heat of water $2256$ kJ/kg. K, specific heat capacity of water $4200$ J/kg. K)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

According to the principle of calorimetry, the heat extracted from one part of the system is equal to the heat absorbed by the other part.

### Step 1: Calculate the heat extracted (lost)

The heat extracted, $Q_{lost}$, from $x$ grams of water when it cools from $50^{\circ}C$ to $0^{\circ}C$ is given by the formula $Q = ms\Delta T$. • Mass, $m = x$ g = $\frac{x}{1000}$ kg • Specific heat capacity of water, $s = 4200$ J/kg.K • Change in temperature, $\Delta T = 50^{\circ}C - 0^{\circ}C = 50$ K $Q_{lost} = \left(\frac{x}{1000}\right)$ \times 4200 \times 50 = 210x $\text{ J}$

### Step 2: Calculate the heat absorbed (gained)

The heat absorbed, $Q_{gained}$, by $(1000-x)$ grams of water initially at $50^{\circ}C$ to evaporate involves two processes: a) Heating the water from $50^{\circ}C$ to its boiling point, $100^{\circ}C$. $Q_1$ = m s $\Delta$ T = $\left(\frac{1000-x}{1000}\right)$ \times 4200 \times (100 - 50) = 210(1000-x) $\text{ J}$ b) Converting the water at $100^{\circ}C$ into steam at $100^{\circ}C$ (latent heat of vaporization). $Q_2$ = m $L_v = \left(\frac{1000-x}{1000}\right)$ \times (2256 \times $10^3$) = 2256(1000-x) $\text{ J}$ Total heat gained is the sum of $Q_1$ and $Q_2$: $Q_{gained} = Q_1 + Q_2$ = 210(1000-x) + 2256(1000-x) $Q_{gained}$ = (210 + 2256)(1000-x) = 2466(1000-x) $\text{ J}$

### Step 3: Equate heat lost and heat gained

$Q_{lost} = Q_{gained}$ 210x = 2466(1000-x)

### Step 4: Solve for x

210x = 2466000 - 2466x 210x + 2466x = 2466000 2676x = 2466000 x = $\frac{2466000}{2676} \approx$ 921.52

### Step 5: Find the closest integer

The question asks for the value of $x$ to the closest integer. Rounding $921.52$ to the nearest integer gives $922$.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
questions.explanation: The definitions and units for the given quantities are as follows: C' = $\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T} = JK^{-1}$ So, Heat capacity of body (A) matches with (II). S = $\frac{\Delta Q}{m\Delta T} = Jkg^{-1} K^{-1}$ So, Specific heat capacity of body (B) matches with (III). L = $\frac{\Delta Q}{m} = Jkg^{-1}$ So, Latent heat (C) matches with (I). $\Delta$ Q = $\frac{KA\Delta T}{L} \Rightarrow$ K = $\frac{\Delta Q(L)}{A\Delta T} = Jm^{-1} K^{-1} s^{-1}$ So, Thermal conductivity (D) matches with (IV). Thus, the correct matching is (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV).

questions.question: On a temperature scale 'X', the boiling point of water is $65^{\circ}$ X and the freezing point is $-15^{\circ}$ X. Assume that the X scale is linear. The equivalent temperature corresponding to $-95^{\circ}$ X on the Fahrenheit scale would be :
questions.explanation: For any linear temperature scale, the relation between two scales X and F is given by the formula: $\frac${$\text{Temperature on X scale} - \text{Freezing point on X scale}$}{$\text{Boiling point on X scale} - \text{Freezing point on X scale}$} = $\frac${$\text{Temperature on F scale} - \text{Freezing point on F scale}$}{$\text{Boiling point on F scale} - \text{Freezing point on F scale}$} Let $X_T$ be the temperature on scale X, $X_L$ be the freezing point on scale X, and $X_H$ be the boiling point on scale X. Similarly, for the Fahrenheit scale, $T_F$ is the temperature, $F_L = 32^{\circ}$ F (freezing point of water), and $F_H = 212^{\circ}$ F (boiling point of water). Given values: • Boiling point on X scale ($X_H$): $65^{\circ}$ X • Freezing point on X scale ($X_L$): $-15^{\circ}$ X • Temperature on X scale to convert ($X_T$): $-95^{\circ}$ X Substitute these values into the formula: $\frac{$X_T - X_L$}{$X_H - X_L$} = \frac{$T_F - F_L$}{$F_H - F_L$} \frac${-$95^{$\circ$}$ - (-$15^{$\circ$}$)}{$65^{$\circ$}$ - (-$15^{$\circ$}$)} = $\frac{$T_F$ - 32}{212 - 32}$ Simplify the numerators and denominators: $\frac${-$95^{$\circ$} + 15^{$\circ$}$}{$65^{$\circ$} + 15^{$\circ$}$} = $\frac{$T_F$ - 32}{180} \frac${-$80^{$\circ$}$}{$80^{$\circ$}$} = $\frac{$T_F$ - 32}{180}$ -1 = $\frac{$T_F$ - 32}{180}$ Multiply both sides by 180 to solve for $T_F$: -1 \times 180 = $T_F$ - 32 -180 = $T_F$ - 32 Add 32 to both sides: $T_F$ = -180 + 32 $T_F$ = -$148^{$\circ$}$ F

questions.question: 10 kg of ice at $-10^{\circ}\text{C}$ is added to 100 kg of water to lower its temperature from $25^{\circ}\text{C}$. Consider no heat exchange to surroundings. The decrement to the temperature of water is __________ $^{\circ}\text{C}$. (specific heat of ice = $2100 \text{ J/Kg}^{\circ}\text{C}$, specific heat of water = $4200 \text{ J/Kg}^{\circ}\text{C}$, latent heat of fusion of ice = $3.36 \times 10^{5} \text{ J/Kg}$)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

According to the principle of calorimetry, the heat lost by the water is equal to the heat gained by the ice, assuming no heat exchange with the surroundings. $\text{Heat Gained by Ice} = \text{Heat Lost by Water}$ Let T be the final equilibrium temperature in $^{\circ}\text{C}$. The heat gained by the ice occurs in three stages: • Heat to raise the temperature of ice from $-10^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $0^{\circ}\text{C}$: $Q_1 = m_{\text{ice}} s_{\text{ice}} \Delta T_1 = 10 \times 2100 \times (0 - (-10)) = 210000 \text{ J}$ • Heat to melt the ice at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ (latent heat of fusion): $Q_2 = m_{\text{ice}} L_f = 10 \times 3.36 \times 10^5 = 3360000 \text{ J}$ • Heat to raise the temperature of the melted ice (now water) from $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to the final temperature T: $Q_3 = m_{\text{ice}} s_{\text{water}} \Delta T_2 = 10 \times 4200 \times (T - 0) = 42000T \text{ J}$ The heat lost by the water as it cools from $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ to T is: Q_{$\text{lost}$} = m_{$\text{water}$} s_{$\text{water}$} $\Delta T_3$ = 100 \times 4200 \times (25 - T) Setting up the heat balance equation: $Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3$ = Q_{$\text{lost}$} 10 \times 3.36 \times $10^5$ + 10 \times 2100 \times 10 + 10 \times 4200 \times (T - 0) = 100 \times 4200 \times (25 - T) 3360000 + 210000 + 42000T = 420000(25 - T) 3570000 + 42000T = 10500000 - 420000T 42000T + 420000T = 10500000 - 3570000 462000T = 6930000 T = $\frac{6930000}{462000} = 15^{$\circ$} \text{C}$ The question asks for the decrement in the temperature of the water, which is the change in its temperature. $\Delta$ T_{$\text{water}$} = T_{$\text{initial}$} - T_{$\text{final}$} = 25 - 15 = $10^{$\circ$} \text{C}$

questions.question: A brass wire of length 2m and radius 1mm at 27°C is held taut between two rigid supports. Initially it was cooled to a temperature of -43°C creating a tension T in the wire. The temperature to which the wire has to be cooled in order to increase the tension in it to 1.4T, is ____ °C
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Express initial tension T

The tension T developed in the wire due to cooling from initial temperature $T_0 = 27^{\circ}C$ to $T_1 = -43^{\circ}C$ is given by the formula: T = $\alpha$ YA ($T_0 - T_1$) Where $\alpha$ is the coefficient of linear expansion, Y is Young's modulus, and A is the cross-sectional area. T = $\alpha$ YA (27 - (-43)) T = $\alpha$ YA (27 + 43) T = $\alpha$ YA (70) $\quad$ \ldots(i)

### Step 2: Express new tension 1.4T

Let the new temperature to which the wire is cooled be $\theta$ to increase the tension to $1.4T$. 1.4T = $\alpha$ YA ($T_0 - \theta$) 1.4T = $\alpha$ YA (27 - $\theta$) $\quad$ \ldots(ii)

### Step 3: Divide equation (ii) by equation (i)

Dividing equation (ii) by equation (i), we get: $\frac{1.4T}{T} = \frac{\alpha YA (27 - \theta)}{\alpha YA (70)}$ 1.4 = $\frac{27 - \theta}{70}$

### Step 4: Solve for $\theta$

Multiply both sides by 70: 1.4 \times 70 = 27 - $\theta$ 98 = 27 - $\theta$ Rearrange to find $\theta$: $\theta$ = 27 - 98 $\theta$ = -$71^{$\circ$}$C

questions.question: The graph between two temperature scales P and Q is shown in the figure. Between upper fixed point and lower fixed point there are 150 equal divisions of scale P and 100 divisions on scale Q. The relationship for conversion between the two scales is given by:--
questions.explanation:
### Understanding Temperature Scales

For any two temperature scales, the relationship between them can be established using the formula: $\frac${$\text{Reading} - \text{Lower Fixed Point (LFP)}$}{$\text{Upper Fixed Point (UFP)} - \text{Lower Fixed Point (LFP)}$} = $\text{constant}$

### Applying the Formula to Scales P and Q

From the given information and the graph: • For scale P: Lower Fixed Point (LFP) $= 30^\circ P$, Upper Fixed Point (UFP) $= 180^\circ P$. The total divisions are $180 - 30 = 150$. • For scale Q: Lower Fixed Point (LFP) $= 0^\circ Q$, Upper Fixed Point (UFP) $= 100^\circ Q$. The total divisions are $100 - 0 = 100$. Using the conversion formula, we equate the expressions for scales P and Q: $\frac${$t_{P} - \text{LFP}_{P}$}{$\text{UFP}_{P} - \text{LFP}_{P}$} = $\frac${$t_{Q} - \text{LFP}_{Q}$}{$\text{UFP}_{Q} - \text{LFP}_{Q}$} $\frac${$t_{P}$ - 30}{180 - 30} = $\frac${$t_{Q}$ - 0}{100 - 0} $\frac${$t_{P}$ - 30}{150} = $\frac${$t_{Q}$}{100} Rearranging the equation to match the given options: $\frac${$t_{Q}$}{100} = $\frac${$t_{P}$ - 30}{150} This relationship matches option (4).

questions.question: Heat energy of 184 kJ is given to ice of mass 600 g at $-12^{\circ}\text{C}$. Specific heat of ice is $2222.3\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{C}^{-1}$ and latent heat of ice in $336\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1}$. A. Final temperature of system will be $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. B. Final temperature of the system will be greater than $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. C. The final system will have a mixture of ice and water in the ratio of $5:1$. D. The final system will have a mixture of ice and water in the ratio of $1:5$. E. The final system will have water only. Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Calculate heat required to raise ice temperature to $0^{\circ}\text{C}$

Given: • Mass of ice $m = 600\ \text{g} = 0.6\ \text{kg}$ • Initial temperature $T_i = -12^{\circ}\text{C}$ • Specific heat of ice $s_{\text{ice}} = 2222.3\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{C}^{-1}$ • Latent heat of fusion of ice $L_f = 336\ \text{kJ kg}^{-1} = 336000\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ • Total heat energy given $Q_{\text{total}} = 184\ \text{kJ} = 184000\ \text{J}$ Heat required to raise the temperature of ice from $-12^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ is $Q_1$: $Q_1$ = m s_{$\text{ice}$} $\Delta$ T = (0.6\ $\text{kg}$) \times (2222.3\ $\text{J kg}^{-1} \text{C}^{-1}$) \times (0 - (-12))^{$\circ$}$\text{C} Q_1$ = 0.6 \times 2222.3 \times 12 = 16000.56\ $\text{J}$

### Step 2: Calculate remaining heat available for melting

Remaining heat $Q_2 = Q_{\text{total}} - Q_1$: $Q_2$ = 184000\ $\text{J}$ - 16000.56\ $\text{J}$ = 167999.44\ $\text{J}$

### Step 3: Calculate heat required to melt all ice

Heat required to melt all $0.6\ \text{kg}$ of ice at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ is $Q_{\text{melt, all}}$: Q_{$\text{melt, all}$} = m $L_f$ = (0.6\ $\text{kg}$) \times (336000\ $\text{J kg}^{-1}$) = 201600\ $\text{J}$

### Step 4: Determine the final state of the system

Since the remaining heat available $Q_2 = 167999.44\ \text{J}$ is less than the heat required to melt all ice $Q_{\text{melt, all}} = 201600\ \text{J}$, not all the ice will melt. Therefore, the final temperature of the system will be $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, and the system will contain a mixture of ice and water. This confirms statement A (Final temperature of system will be $0^{\circ}\text{C}$).

### Step 5: Calculate the mass of water formed and remaining ice

Mass of ice melted (which becomes water) $m_{\text{water}}$: $Q_2$ = m_{$\text{water}$} $L_f$ 167999.44\ $\text{J}$ = m_{$\text{water}$} \times 336000\ $\text{J kg}^{-1}$ m_{$\text{water}$} = $\frac{167999.44}{336000} \approx$ 0.499998\ $\text{kg} \approx$ 0.5\ $\text{kg}$ Mass of remaining ice $m_{\text{ice}} = \text{Total mass of ice} - m_{\text{water}}$: m_{$\text{ice}$} = 0.6\ $\text{kg}$ - 0.499998\ $\text{kg}$ = 0.100002\ $\text{kg} \approx$ 0.1\ $\text{kg}$

### Step 6: Determine the ratio of ice to water

The ratio of ice to water is $m_{\text{ice}} : m_{\text{water}}$: $\text{Ratio} = \frac${m_{$\text{ice}$}}{m_{$\text{water}$}} = $\frac{0.100002}{0.499998} \approx \frac{1}{5}$ So, the ratio of ice to water is approximately $1:5$. This confirms statement D (The final system will have a mixture of ice and water in the ratio of $1:5$).

### Step 7: Conclusion

Based on the analysis, statements A and D are correct. Therefore, the correct option is (1) A and D Only.

questions.question: A faulty thermometer reads $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ in melting ice and $95^{\circ}\text{C}$ in stream. The correct temperature on absolute scale will be ______ K when the faulty thermometer reads $41^{\circ}\text{C}$.
questions.explanation: The principle for relating two temperature scales is that the ratio of the difference between a temperature reading and the lower fixed point to the difference between the upper fixed point and the lower fixed point is constant for both scales. For the faulty thermometer: • Lower Fixed Point (LFP) = $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ • Upper Fixed Point (UFP) = $95^{\circ}\text{C}$ For the standard Celsius scale: • Lower Fixed Point (LFP) = $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ (melting ice) • Upper Fixed Point (UFP) = $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ (steam point) Let $R$ be the correct temperature in Celsius when the faulty thermometer reads $41^{\circ}\text{C}$. Using the relation: $\frac${$\text{Faulty reading} - \text{LFP}$_{$\text{faulty}$}}{$\text{UFP}$_{$\text{faulty}$} - $\text{LFP}$_{$\text{faulty}$}} = $\frac${$\text{Celsius reading} - \text{LFP}$_{$\text{Celsius}$}}{$\text{UFP}$_{$\text{Celsius}$} - $\text{LFP}$_{$\text{Celsius}$}} $\frac${$41^{$\circ$} - 5^{$\circ$}$}{$95^{$\circ$} - 5^{$\circ$}$} = $\frac{R - 0}{100 - 0} \frac{36}{90} = \frac{R}{100} \frac{2}{5} = \frac{R}{100}$ R = $\frac{2}{5}$ \times 100 R = $40^{$\circ$} \text{C}$ To convert temperature from Celsius to Kelvin, we use the formula: T_{$\text{K}$} = T_{$\text{C}$} + 273.15 Using $T_{\text{C}} = 40^{\circ}\text{C}$: T_{$\text{K}$} = 40 + 273 T_{$\text{K}$} = 313$\text{ K}$

questions.question: Consider a rectangular sheet of solid material of length $l = 9$ cm and width $d = 4$ cm. The coefficient of linear expansion is $\alpha = 3.1 \times 10^{-5}$ K$^{-1}$ at room temperature and one atmospheric pressure. The mass of sheet $m = 0.1$ kg and the specific heat capacity $C_{v} = 900$ J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. If the amount of heat supplied to the material is $8.1 \times 10^{2}$ J then change in area of the rectangular sheet is :-
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Calculate the change in temperature ($\Delta T$)

The amount of heat supplied ($\Delta Q$) is related to the mass ($m$), specific heat capacity ($C_v$), and change in temperature ($\Delta T$) by the formula: $\Delta$ Q = m $C_v \Delta$ T Given $\Delta Q = 8.1 \times 10^{2}$ J, $m = 0.1$ kg, and $C_v = 900$ J kg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$. Substitute these values: 8.1 \times $10^{2}$ = 0.1 \times 900 \times $\Delta$ T 810 = 90 \times $\Delta$ T Solve for $\Delta T$: $\Delta$ T = $\frac{810}{90}$ = 9$\text{ K}$

### Step 2: Calculate the initial area ($A_0$)

The rectangular sheet has length $l = 9$ cm and width $d = 4$ cm. The initial area $A_0$ is: $A_0$ = l \times d = 9$\text{ cm}$ \times 4$\text{ cm}$ = 36$\text{ cm}^2$ Convert the initial area to square meters: $A_0$ = 36 \times ($10^{-2} \text{ m}$)^2 = 36 \times $10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$

### Step 3: Calculate the change in area ($\Delta A$)

The coefficient of area expansion ($\beta$) is twice the coefficient of linear expansion ($\alpha$), i.e., $\beta = 2\alpha$. The change in area ($\Delta A$) is given by: $\Delta$ A = $A_0 \beta \Delta$ T = $A_0$ (2$\alpha$) $\Delta$ T Given $\alpha = 3.1 \times 10^{-5}$ K$^{-1}$. Substitute the values of $A_0$, $\alpha$, and $\Delta T$: $\Delta$ A = (36 \times $10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$) \times (2 \times 3.1 \times $10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$) \times (9$\text{ K}$) $\Delta$ A = (36 \times 6.2 \times 9) \times $10^{-4}$ \times $10^{-5} \text{ m}^2 \Delta$ A = (223.2 \times 9) \times $10^{-9} \text{ m}^2 \Delta$ A = 2008.8 \times $10^{-9} \text{ m}^2$ Rounding to one significant figure, the change in area is: $\Delta$ A $\approx$ 2.0 \times $10^{-6} \text{ m}^2$

questions.question: An ideal gas at pressure $P$ and temperature $T$ is expanding such that $PT^3 = \text{constant}$. The coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is _______.
questions.explanation: Given the relation for the ideal gas expansion: $PT^3 = \text{constant (C)}$ From the ideal gas law, $PV = nRT$, we can express pressure $P$ as: P = $\frac{nRT}{V}$ Substitute the expression for $P$ into the given relation: $\left(\frac{nRT}{V}\right) T^3$ = C Rearrange the equation to express $V$ in terms of $T$: $\frac{$nRT^4$}{V}$ = C $\implies$ V = $\frac{nR}{C} T^4$ The coefficient of volume expansion ($\gamma$) is defined as: $\gamma = \frac{1}{V} \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)$_P In this case, since $V$ is a function of $T$ only (as $n, R, C$ are constants), we can write $\frac{dV}{dT}$. First, differentiate $V$ with respect to $T$: $\frac{dV}{dT} = \frac{d}{dT}\left(\frac{nR}{C} T^4\right) = \frac{nR}{C}$ ($4T^3$) Now, substitute $V$ and $\frac{dV}{dT}$ into the formula for $\gamma$: $\gamma = \frac{1}{\left(\frac{nR}{C} T^4\right)$} $\left(\frac{nR}{C} 4T^3\right)$ Simplify the expression: $\gamma = \frac{C}{nR $T^4$}$ \cdot $\frac{nR \cdot $4T^3$}{C} = \frac{$4T^3$}{$T^4$} = \frac{4}{T}$ Thus, the coefficient of volume expansion of the gas is $\frac{4}{T}$.

questions.question: The resistances of the platinum wire of a platinum resistance thermometer at the ice point and steam point are $8 \Omega$ and $10 \Omega$ respectively. After inserting in a hot bath of temperature $400^{\circ}\text{C}$, the resistance of platinum wire is :
questions.explanation: Given, $R_{0}$ = 8$\Omega$ And $R_{100}$ = 10$\Omega \frac{C - 0}{100} = \frac${R - $R_{0}$}{$R_{100} - R_{0}$} $\Rightarrow \frac{400}{100} = \frac{R - 8}{2} \Rightarrow$ R - 8 = 8 $\Rightarrow$ R = 16 $\Omega$

questions.question: An aluminium and steel rods having same lengths and cross-sections are joined to make total length of 120 cm at 30°C. The coefficient of linear expansion of aluminium and steel are $24 \times 10^{-6}/^{\circ}C$ and $1.2 \times 10^{-5}/^{\circ}C$, respectively. The length of this composite rod when its temperature is raised to 100°C, is ________ cm.
questions.explanation: Given that the total length of the composite rod is 120 cm, and the aluminium and steel rods have the same length, the initial length of each rod ($\ell_0$) is: $\$ell_0  = $\frac{120}{2}$ = 60 $\text{ cm}$ The initial temperature is $T_i = 30^{\circ}C$ and the final temperature is $T_f = 100^{\circ}C$. The change in temperature ($\Delta T$) is: $\Delta$ T = $T_f - T_i = 100^{$\circ$}$C - $30^{$\circ$}$C = $70^{$\circ$}$C The coefficients of linear expansion are: $\$alpha_{A}  = 24 \times $10^{-6}$ /^{$\circ$}C $\quad$ ($\text{Aluminium}$) $\$alpha_{B}  = 1.2 \times $10^{-5}$ /^{$\circ$}C = 12 \times $10^{-6}$ /^{$\circ$}C $\quad$ ($\text{Steel}$) The final length of the composite rod is the sum of the final lengths of the individual rods: $\ell$_{$\text{final}$} = $\ell$_{A, $\text{final}$} + $\ell$_{B, $\text{final}$} $\ell$_{$\text{final}$} = $\$ell_{0} (1 + $\$alpha_{A}$$$\Delta$ T) + $\$ell_{0} (1 + $\$alpha_{B}$$$\Delta$ T) Simplifying the expression: $\ell$_{$\text{final}$} = $\$ell_{0}$[ (1 + \$alpha_{A}$\Delta T) + (1 + \$alpha_{B}$\Delta T) ] \ell$_{$\text{final}$} = $\$ell_{0}$[2 + (\$alpha_{A}$ + \$alpha_{B}$)\Delta T]$ Now, substitute the values: $\ell$_{$\text{final}$} = 60[2 + (24 \times $10^{-6}$ + 12 \times $10^{-6}$) \times 70] = 60[2 + (36 \times $10^{-6}$) \times 70] = 60[2 + 2520 \times $10^{-6}$] = 60[2 + 0.00252] = 60[2.00252] = 120.1512 $\text{ cm}$ Rounding to two decimal places, the final length is 120.15 cm.

questions.question: A block of ice at $-10^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ is slowly heated and converted to steam at $100^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. Which of the following curves represent the phenomenon qualitatively:

questions.question: A gas based geyser heats water flowing at the rate of $5.0$ litres per minute from $27^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $87^{\circ}\text{C}$. The rate of consumption of the gas is ____ g/s. (Take heat of combustion of gas = $5.0 \times 10^4$ J/g) specific heat capacity of water = $4200$ J/kg. $^{\circ}\text{C}$
questions.explanation: Water flow rate = $5$ l/min = $\frac{5}{60}$ kg/s $\therefore \text{Power of heater} = \frac{dm}{dt}$ S$\Delta$ T = $\frac{1}{12}$ \times 4200 \times 60$\text{W} \therefore$ Let rate of consumption of gas be $x$ g/s. $\therefore$ x \times 5.0 \times $10^4 = \frac{1}{12}$ \times 4200 \times 60 $\Rightarrow$ x = 4200 \times $10^{-4}$ = 0.42$\text{ g/s}$

questions.question: A body cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $5$ minutes. The temperature of the surrounding is $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. The time it takes to cool from $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ is:
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

### Step 1: State Newton's Law of Cooling and identify given values

A body cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $5$ minutes. The surrounding temperature is $T_{\text{surrounding}} = \theta_{0} = 20^{\circ}\text{C}$. Newton's Law of Cooling states that the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings: -$\frac{d\theta}{dt}$ = b($\theta - \$theta_{0} ) For approximate calculations over a finite time interval $\Delta t$, we can write: $\frac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}$ = b($\theta$_{$\text{avg}$} - $\$theta_{0} )

### Step 2: Calculate the constant 'b' for the first cooling phase

For the first cooling phase (from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $5$ minutes): Temperature change $\Delta\theta = 80^{\circ}\text{C} - 60^{\circ}\text{C} = 20^{\circ}\text{C}$. Time interval $\Delta t = 5$ minutes. Average temperature $\theta_{\text{avg1}} = \frac{80^{\circ}\text{C} + 60^{\circ}\text{C}}{2} = 70^{\circ}\text{C}$. Substituting these values into the approximate Newton's Law of Cooling equation: $\frac{20}{5}$ = b(70 - 20) 4 = b(50) b = $\frac{4}{50} = \frac{2}{25} \text{ min}^{-1}$

### Step 3: Calculate the time 't' for the second cooling phase

For the second cooling phase (from $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$): Temperature change $\Delta\theta = 60^{\circ}\text{C} - 40^{\circ}\text{C} = 20^{\circ}\text{C}$. Let the time taken be $t$ minutes. Average temperature $\theta_{\text{avg2}} = \frac{60^{\circ}\text{C} + 40^{\circ}\text{C}}{2} = 50^{\circ}\text{C}$. Using the same equation with the calculated value of $b$: $\frac{20}{t}$ = b(50 - 20) $\frac{20}{t} = \frac{2}{25}$ (30) $\frac{20}{t} = \frac{60}{25}$ t = $\frac{20 \times 25}{60}$ t = $\frac{500}{60} = \frac{50}{6} = \frac{25}{3} \text{ minutes}$

### Step 4: Convert the time from minutes to seconds

To convert minutes to seconds, multiply by $60$: t = $\frac{25}{3}$ \times 60 $\text{ seconds}$ t = 25 \times 20 $\text{ seconds}$ t = 500 $\text{ seconds}$ The time it takes to cool from $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $40^{\circ}\text{C}$ is $500$ s.

questions.question: An amount of ice of mass $10^{-3}$ kg and temperature $-10^{\circ}$C is transformed to vapour of temperature $110^{\circ}$ by applying heat. The total amount of work required for this conversion is, (Take, specific heat of ice = $2100$ Jkg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, specific heat of water = $4180$ Jkg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, specific heat of steam = $1920$ Jkg$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, Latent heat of ice = $3.35 \times 10^5$ Jkg$^{-1}$ and Latent heat of steam = $2.25 \times 10^6$ Jkg$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Identify the different phases of heat absorption

The process involves several stages of heat absorption as ice at $-10^{\circ}$C is converted to steam at $110^{\circ}$C: • Heating ice from $-10^{\circ}$C to $0^{\circ}$C ($\Delta Q_1$) • Melting ice at $0^{\circ}$C to water at $0^{\circ}$C ($\Delta Q_2$) • Heating water from $0^{\circ}$C to $100^{\circ}$C ($\Delta Q_3$) • Vaporizing water at $100^{\circ}$C to steam at $100^{\circ}$C ($\Delta Q_4$) • Heating steam from $100^{\circ}$C to $110^{\circ}$C ($\Delta Q_5$)

### Step 2: Calculate heat absorbed in each stage

Given mass $m = 10^{-3}$ kg. $\Delta Q_1$ = m \times $S_i$ \times $\Delta$ T = $10^{-3}$ \times 2100 \times (0 - (-10)) = $10^{-3}$ \times 2100 \times 10 = 21 J $\Delta Q_2$ = m \times $L_f = 10^{-3}$ \times 3.35 \times $10^5$ = 335 J $\Delta Q_3$ = m \times $S_w$ \times $\Delta$ T = $10^{-3}$ \times 4180 \times (100 - 0) = $10^{-3}$ \times 4180 \times 100 = 418 J $\Delta Q_4$ = m \times $L_v = 10^{-3}$ \times 2.25 \times $10^6$ = 2250 J $\Delta Q_5$ = m \times $S_v$ \times $\Delta$ T = $10^{-3}$ \times 1920 \times (110 - 100) = $10^{-3}$ \times 1920 \times 10 = 19.2 J

### Step 3: Calculate the total heat absorbed

The total heat required (work done) is the sum of all these heat quantities: $\Delta Q_{net} = \Delta Q_1 + \Delta Q_2 + \Delta Q_3 + \Delta Q_4 + \Delta Q_5 \Delta Q_{net}$ = 21 + 335 + 418 + 2250 + 19.2 = 3043.2 J The total amount of work required for this conversion is approximately 3043 J.

questions.question: Which of the following figure represents the relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit temperatures?
questions.explanation:
### Step 1: Recall the conversion formula between Celsius and Fahrenheit.

The standard formula relating Celsius ($C$) and Fahrenheit ($F$) temperatures is: $\frac{C}{5} = \frac{F - 32}{9}$

### Step 2: Rearrange the formula to express C in terms of F.

Multiplying both sides by 5, we get: C = $\frac{5}{9}$(F - 32) Expanding this equation: C = $\frac{5F}{9} - \frac{5 \times 32}{9}$ C = $\frac{5F}{9} - \frac{160}{9}$

### Step 3: Analyze the characteristics of the linear equation.

This equation is in the form $y = mx + c$, where $y = C$ and $x = F$. • The slope $m = \frac{5}{9}$. Since $m > 0$, the graph must have a positive slope (an upward trend from left to right). • The C-intercept (y-intercept) is $c = -\frac{160}{9}$. Since $c < 0$, the line must intersect the C-axis (y-axis) at a negative value. • To find the F-intercept (x-intercept), set $C = 0$: $0 = \frac{5F}{9} - \frac{160}{9} \Rightarrow \frac{5F}{9} = \frac{160}{9} \Rightarrow 5F = 160 \Rightarrow F = 32$. So, the line intersects the F-axis (x-axis) at a positive value (32).

### Step 4: Match the characteristics with the given figures.

Based on the analysis: • The graph must have a positive slope. • The graph must intersect the C-axis at a negative value. • The graph must intersect the F-axis at a positive value. Figure (2) correctly represents these characteristics: Thus, figure (2) represents the correct relation.

questions.question: The pressure (P) and temperature (T) relationship of an ideal gas obeys the equation $PT^2 = \text{constant}$. The volume expansion coefficient of the gas will be :
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

$PT^2 = \text{const.}$ dV = V$\gamma$ dT $\gamma = \frac{1}{V} \frac{dV}{dT} \quad$ ...(1) Using $PV = nRT$ and $PT^2 = \text{const.} \frac{nRT}{V}$ \cdot $T^2 = \text{const}$ V $\propto T^3 \implies$ V = $KT^3 \quad$ ...(2) Now put in (1) $\gamma = \frac{1}{$KT^3$}$ \times $3KT^2 = \frac{3}{T} \implies \gamma = \frac{3}{T}$

questions.question: On celcius scale the temperature of body increases by $40^{\circ}\text{C}$. The increase in temperature on Fahrenheit scale is -
questions.explanation: $\frac{C - 0}{100} = \frac{F - 32}{180}$ C = $\frac{5}{9}$(F - 32) $\Delta$ C = $\frac{5}{9} \Delta$ F 40 = $\frac{5}{9} \Delta$ F $\Rightarrow \Delta$ F = $72^{$\circ$} \text{F}$

questions.question: The temperature of a metal strip having coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$ is increased from $T_{1}$ to $T_{2}$ resulting in increase of its length by $\Delta L_{1}$. The temperature is further increased from $T_{2}$ to $T_{3}$ such that the increase in its length is $\Delta L_{2}$. Given $T_{3} + T_{1} = 2T_{2}$ and $T_{2} - T_{1} = \Delta T$, the value of $\Delta L_{2}$ is $ \underline{\hspace{2cm}} $.
questions.explanation:
Let the initial length of the metal strip be $L_{0}$.

### Step 1: Calculate $\Delta L_{1}$

When the temperature increases from $T_{1}$ to $T_{2}$, the increase in length is given by: $\Delta L_{1} = L_{0} \alpha$ ($T_{2} - T_{1}$) Given $T_{2} - T_{1} = \Delta T$, so: $\Delta L_{1} = L_{0} \alpha \Delta$ T $\quad$ \ldots (1)

### Step 2: Determine the length at $T_{2}$

The final length at temperature $T_{2}$ is $L_{0}' = L_{0} + \Delta L_{1}$.

### Step 3: Calculate $\Delta L_{2}$

When the temperature further increases from $T_{2}$ to $T_{3}$, the increase in length $\Delta L_{2}$ is based on the length at $T_{2}$: $\Delta L_{2} = L_{0}$' $\alpha$ ($T_{3} - T_{2}$) Substitute $L_{0}' = L_{0} + \Delta L_{1}$: $\Delta L_{2}$ = ($L_{0} + \Delta L_{1}$) $\alpha$ ($T_{3} - T_{2}$)

### Step 4: Use the given temperature relations

We are given $T_{3} + T_{1} = 2T_{2}$ and $T_{2} - T_{1} = \Delta T$. From $T_{3} + T_{1} = 2T_{2}$, we can rearrange to find $T_{3} - T_{2}$: $T_{3} - T_{2} = T_{2} - T_{1}$ Since $T_{2} - T_{1} = \Delta T$, it implies: $T_{3} - T_{2} = \Delta$ T

### Step 5: Substitute and simplify for $\Delta L_{2}$

Substitute $T_{3} - T_{2} = \Delta T$ into the expression for $\Delta L_{2}$: $\Delta L_{2}$ = ($L_{0} + \Delta L_{1}$) $\alpha \Delta$ T Expand the expression: $\Delta L_{2} = L_{0} \alpha \Delta$ T + $\Delta L_{1} \alpha \Delta$ T From equation (1), we know that $L_{0} \alpha \Delta T = \Delta L_{1}$. Substitute this back into the equation for $\Delta L_{2}$: $\Delta L_{2} = \Delta L_{1} + \Delta L_{1} \alpha \Delta$ T Factor out $\Delta L_{1}$: $\Delta L_{2} = \Delta L_{1}$ (1 + $\alpha \Delta$ T)

questions.question: A gun fires a lead bullet of temperature 300K into a wooden block. The bullet having melting temperature of 600 K penetrates into the block and melts down. If the total heat required for the process is 625 J, then the mass of the bullet is ____ grams. (Latent heat of fusion of lead = $2.5 \times 10^4 \text{ JKg}^{-1}$ and specific heat capacity of lead = $125 \text{ JKg}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: The total heat required for the process is the sum of the heat required to raise the temperature of the bullet to its melting point and the heat required to melt the bullet. Q = ms$\Delta$ T + mL Given values: • Initial temperature $T_1 = 300\text{ K}$ • Melting temperature $T_2 = 600\text{ K}$ • Total heat required $Q = 625\text{ J}$ • Specific heat capacity of lead $s = 125\text{ JKg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ • Latent heat of fusion of lead $L = 2.5 \times 10^4 \text{ JKg}^{-1}$ Substitute the values into the equation: 625 = m[125 \times (600 - 300) + 2.5 \times $10^4$] 625 = m[125 \times 300 + 2.5 \times $10^4$] 625 = m[37500 + 25000] 625 = m[62500] Now, solve for $m$: m = $\frac{625}{62500} \text{ kg}$ m = $\frac{1}{100} \text{ kg}$ To convert the mass from kilograms to grams, multiply by 1000: m = $\frac{1}{100}$ \times 1000 $\text{ grams}$ m = 10 $\text{ grams}$

questions.question: A body cools from 60°C to 40°C in 6 minutes. If, temperature of surroundings is 10°C. Then, after the next 6 minutes, its temperature will be °C.
questions.explanation:
### Applying Newton's Law of Cooling

Newton's Law of Cooling states that the rate of cooling of a body is directly proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings. The formula is given by: $\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}$ = k(T_{$\text{avg}$} - $T_0$) Where $\Delta T$ is the change in temperature, $\Delta t$ is the time taken, $k$ is a constant, $T_{\text{avg}}$ is the average temperature of the body during the interval, and $T_0$ is the temperature of the surroundings. Given $T_0 = 10^{\circ}C$.

### For the first cooling interval (60°C to 40°C in 6 minutes)

Here, $\Delta T = 60 - 40 = 20^{\circ}C$, $\Delta t = 6$ minutes, and $T_{\text{avg}} = \frac{60 + 40}{2} = 50^{\circ}C$. $\frac{60 - 40}{6}$ = k $\left[ \frac{60 + 40}{2} - 10 \right] \frac{20}{6}$ = k[50 - 10] $\frac{20}{6}$ = k[40] $\quad$ \ldots(1)

### For the second cooling interval (40°C to T in the next 6 minutes)

Here, $\Delta T = 40 - T$, $\Delta t = 6$ minutes, and $T_{\text{avg}} = \frac{40 + T}{2}$. $\frac{40 - T}{6}$ = k $\left[ \frac{40 + T}{2} - 10 \right] \quad$ \ldots(2)

### Dividing equation (1) by equation (2)

$\frac${$\frac{20}{6}$}{$\frac{40 - T}{6}$} = $\frac{k[40]}${k $\left[ \frac{40 + T}{2} - 10 \right]$} $\frac{20}{40 - T} = \frac{40}${$\frac{40 + T - 20}{2}$} $\frac{20}{40 - T} = \frac{40 \times 2}{20 + T} \frac{20}{40 - T} = \frac{80}{20 + T}$ Cross-multiplying and simplifying: 20(20 + T) = 80(40 - T) 20 + T = 4(40 - T) 20 + T = 160 - 4T T + 4T = 160 - 20 5T = 140 T = $\frac{140}{5}$ T = $28^{$\circ$}$C The temperature of the body after the next 6 minutes will be 28°C.

questions.question: In a perfectly inelastic collision, two spheres made of the same material with masses 15 kg and 25 kg, moving in opposite directions with speeds of 10 m/s and 30 m/s, respectively, strike each other and stick together. The rise in temperature (in $^{\circ}\text{C}$), if all the heat produced during the collision is retained by these spheres, is : (specific heat of sphere material 31 cal/kg. $^{\circ}\text{C}$ and 1 cal = 4.2 J)
questions.explanation:
### Detailed Solution

### Step 1: Calculate the loss in kinetic energy

(K.E)_{$\text{lost}$} = $\frac{1}{2} \mu$ V_{$\text{rel}$}^2 (1-$e^2$) =$ \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{m_{1} m_{2}}{m_{1} + m_{2}} \right)$ (10+30)^2 (1-0) =$ \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{(15)(25)}{15+25} \right]$ [40]$^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \frac{375}{40} \right]$ [1600] = $\frac{1}{2}$ \times 9.375 \times 1600 = 7500 $\text{ J}$

### Step 2: Relate kinetic energy loss to heat gained and temperature rise

The heat produced during the collision is equal to the loss in kinetic energy, and this heat is retained by the spheres, causing a rise in temperature. (K.E)_{$\text{loss}$} = ($m_{1} + m_{2}$) (S) ($\Delta$ T) Given specific heat $S = 31 \text{ cal/kg-}^{\circ}\text{C}$. We need to convert this to J/kg-${^{\circ}\text{C}}$. S = 31 \times 4.2 $\text{ J/kg-}^{\circ} \text{C}$ 7500 = (15 + 25) (31 \times 4.2) ($\Delta$ T) 7500 = (40) (31 \times 4.2) ($\Delta$ T)

### Step 3: Calculate the rise in temperature

$\Delta$ T = $\frac{7500}{40 \times 31 \times 4.2} \Delta$ T = $\frac{7500}{1240 \times 4.2} \Delta$ T = $\frac{7500}{5208} \Delta$ T $\approx$ 1.$4405^{$\circ$} \text{C}$ Rounding to two decimal places, the rise in temperature is $1.44^{\circ}\text{C}$.

questions.question: A water heater of power 2000 W is used to heat water. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J $kg^{-1} K^{-1}$. The efficiency of heater is 70%. Time required to heat 2 kg of water from $10^{\circ}C$ to $60^{\circ}C$ is ______ s. (Assume that the specific heat capacity of water remains constant over the temperature range of the water).
questions.explanation: P_{$\text{used}$} = 0.7 \times 2000 = 1400$\text{W}$ P = $\frac{ms\Delta T}{t}$ t = $\frac{2 \times 4200 \times (60-10)}{1400}$ t = $\frac{2 \times 4200 \times 50}{1400}$ t = 300 $\text{ sec}$

questions.question: Which of the following best represents the temperature versus heat supplied graph for water, in the range of -20°C to 120°C ?
questions.explanation:
### Analysis of the Heating Curve for Water

The process of heating water from -20°C to 120°C involves changes in temperature and phase. The temperature versus heat supplied graph illustrates these changes.

### Step-by-step process:

• **Heating Ice (-20°C to 0°C):** Heat is supplied to solid ice, and its temperature rises. The graph shows a line with a positive slope. • **Melting Ice (at 0°C):** At 0°C, the ice starts to melt into water. During this phase change, the temperature remains constant even though heat is being supplied. This is represented by a horizontal line on the graph. • **Heating Water (0°C to 100°C):** Once all the ice has melted, the temperature of the liquid water rises as more heat is supplied. This is shown as another line with a positive slope. • **Boiling Water (at 100°C):** At 100°C, the water begins to boil and turn into steam. The temperature remains constant during this phase change, which is represented by another horizontal line. • **Heating Steam (100°C to 120°C):** After all the water has turned into steam, the temperature of the steam rises with further heat supply. Graph (2) is the only one that correctly shows these five distinct stages: three sloped sections representing temperature increases and two horizontal plateaus at 0°C and 100°C representing the phase changes (melting and boiling). Furthermore, the slope of the temperature-heat graph is given by $\frac{dT}{dQ} = \frac{1}{ms}$, where $m$ is the mass and $s$ is the specific heat capacity. Since the specific heat of water ($s_{water} \approx 4.2 \, J/g°C$) is roughly twice that of ice ($s_{ice} \approx 2.1 \, J/g°C$) and steam ($s_{steam} \approx 2.0 \, J/g°C$), the slope for the liquid water phase (0°C to 100°C) should be the smallest (least steep). Graph (2) correctly reflects this detail.

questions.question: Water falls from a height of 200 m into a pool. Calculate the rise in temperature of the water assuming no heat dissipation from the water in the pool. (Take $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, specific heat of water $= 4200 \text{ J/(kg K)}$)
questions.explanation: When water falls from a height, its potential energy is converted into heat energy, which causes a rise in temperature. Assuming no heat dissipation, the potential energy lost by the water is equal to the heat gained by the water. mgh = ms$\Delta$ T Where: • $m$ = mass of water • $g$ = acceleration due to gravity $= 10 \text{ m/s}^2$ • $h$ = height $= 200 \text{ m}$ • $s$ = specific heat of water $= 4200 \text{ J/(kg K)}$ • $\Delta T$ = rise in temperature From the equation, we can find the rise in temperature $\Delta T$: $\Delta$ T = $\frac{gh}{s}$ Substitute the given values: $\Delta$ T = $\frac{10 \times 200}{4200} \text{ K} \Delta$ T = $\frac{2000}{4200} \text{ K} \Delta$ T = $\frac{20}{42} \text{ K} \Delta$ T = $\frac{10}{21} \text{ K}$ Now, calculate the numerical value: $\Delta$ T $\approx$ 0.47619 $\text{ K}$ Rounding to two decimal places, the rise in temperature is approximately $0.48 \text{ K}$.

questions.question: A current carrying wire heats a metal rod. The wire provides a constant power $P$ to the rod. The metal rod is enclosed in an insulated container. It is observed that the temperature $T$ in the metal rod changes with time $t$ as : T(t) = $T_{0}$ (1 + $\beta t^{1/4}$) where $\beta$ is a constant with appropriate dimension while $T_{0}$ is a constant with dimension of temperature. The heat capacity of the metal is :
questions.explanation: Given, power $P = \frac{dQ}{dt}$. Also, $dQ = S dT$, where $S$ is the heat capacity. $\frac{dQ}{dt}$ = S $\frac{dT}{dt} \implies S = \frac{P}{\left(\frac{dT}{dt}\right)$} Given temperature variation with time: T(t) = $T_{0}$ (1 + $\beta t^{1/4}$) Differentiating $T(t)$ with respect to $t$: $\frac{dT}{dt} = T_{0} \left[0 + \beta \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot t^{(1/4)-1}\right] = T_{0} \left[\frac{\beta}{4} t^{-3/4}\right] = \frac${$\beta T_{0}$}{4} $t^{-3/4}$ Substitute $\frac{dT}{dt}$ into the expression for $S$: S = $\frac{P}${$\frac${$\beta T_{0}$}{4} $t^{-3/4}$} = $\frac{4P}${$\beta T_{0}$} $t^{3/4}$ From the given temperature equation, we can express $t^{3/4}$ in terms of $T(t)$ and $T_{0}$: $\frac{T(t)}${$T_{0}$} = 1 + $\beta t^{1/4} \beta t^{1/4} = \frac{T(t)}${$T_{0}$} - 1 = $\frac${T(t) - $T_{0}$}{$T_{0}$} $t^{1/4} = \frac${T(t) - $T_{0}$}{$\beta T_{0}$} Cubing both sides to get $t^{3/4}$: $t^{3/4} = \left(\frac{T(t) - T_{0}}{\beta T_{0}}\right)$^{3} Now substitute this expression for $t^{3/4}$ back into the equation for $S$: S = $\frac{4P}${$\beta T_{0}$} $\left[\frac{T(t) - T_{0}}{\beta T_{0}}\right]$^{3} S = $\frac{4P}${$\beta T_{0}$} $\frac${(T(t) - $T_{0}$)^{3}}{$\$beta^{3}  $T_{0}^{3}$} S = $\frac${4P(T(t) - $T_{0}$)^{3}}{$\$beta^{4}  $T_{0}^{4}$} This matches option (1).

questions.question: A water cooler of storage capacity 120 litres can cool water at a constant rate of $P$ watts. In a closed circulation system (as shown schematically in the figure), the water from the cooler is used to cool an external device that generates constantly 3 kW of heat (thermal load). The temperature of water fed into the device cannot exceed $30 \,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and the entire stored 120 litres of water is initially cooled to $10 \,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The entire system is thermally insulated. The minimum value of $P$ (in watts) for which the device can be operated for 3 hours is (Specific heat of water is $4.2 \,\mathrm{kJ}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ and the density of water is $1000 \,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$)
questions.explanation:
### Understanding the problem and given values

The water cooler has a storage capacity of $V = 120$ litres. It cools water at a constant rate of $P$ watts. The external device generates $P_{\mathrm{heater}} = 3\,\mathrm{kW} = 3 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{W}$ of heat. The maximum temperature of water fed into the device is $T_{\mathrm{max}} = 30 \,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The initial temperature of the stored water is $T_{\mathrm{initial}} = 10 \,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. The system operates for $t = 3$ hours. Specific heat of water $c = 4.2 \,\mathrm{kJ}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1} = 4.2 \times 10^3 \,\mathrm{J}\,\mathrm{kg}^{-1}\,\mathrm{K}^{-1}$. Density of water $\rho = 1000 \,\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

### Calculating the mass of water

The volume of water is $120$ litres. Since $1$ litre $= 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^3$, the volume is $V = 120 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m}^3$. The mass of water is $m = \rho V$. m = 1000 \,$\mathrm{kg}$\,$\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ \times 120 \times $10^{-3}$\,$\mathrm{m}^3$ = 120 \,$\mathrm{kg}$

### Calculating the total time in seconds

t = 3 \,$\mathrm{hours}$ = 3 \times 3600 \,$\mathrm{seconds}$ = 10800 \,$\mathrm{s}$

### Determining the temperature change

The water is initially at $10 \,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and can heat up to $30 \,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. So, the maximum permissible temperature change is $\Delta T = T_{\mathrm{max}} - T_{\mathrm{initial}}$. $\Delta$ T = 30 \,^{$\circ$}$\mathrm{C}$ - 10 \,^{$\circ$}$\mathrm{C}$ = 20 \,^{$\circ$}$\mathrm{C}$ = 20 \,$\mathrm{K}$

### Applying the energy balance equation

The net heat absorbed by the water over time $t$ is equal to the heat generated by the device minus the heat removed by the cooler. This net heat causes the temperature of the water to rise. The equation for energy balance is: (P_{$\mathrm{heater}$} - P) \times t = m c $\Delta$ T Substitute the known values into the equation: (3 \times $10^3$ - P) \times (3 \times 3600) = 120 \times (4.2 \times $10^3$) \times 20 (3000 - P) \times 10800 = 120 \times 4200 \times 20 (3000 - P) \times 10800 = 10080000 3000 - P = $\frac{10080000}{10800}$ 3000 - P = 933.333... P = 3000 - 933.333... P = 2066.666... \,$\mathrm{W}$ Rounding to the nearest integer, the minimum value of $P$ is $2067$ watts. The minimum value of P is 2067 W.

questions.question: The specific heat capacity of a substance is temperature dependent and is given by the formula $C = kT$, where $k$ is a constant of suitable dimensions in SI units, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. If the heat required to raise the temperature of 1 kg of the substance from $-73^{\circ}C$ to $27^{\circ}C$ is $nk$, the value of $n$ is _______. [Given: $0 K = -273^{\circ}C$.]
questions.explanation: Sol. The specific heat capacity is given by: C = $\frac{dQ/m}{dT}$ Rearranging for $dQ$: $\Rightarrow$ dQ = m \cdot C \cdot dT Given $m = 1$ kg and $C = kT$: = 1 \cdot kTdT Convert temperatures to Kelvin: $T_1 = -73^{\circ}C = -73 + 273 = 200 K T_2 = 27^{\circ}C = 27 + 273 = 300 K$ Integrate $dQ$ to find the total heat $Q$: Q = $\$int_{200}^{300}  kTdT = k $\left[ \frac{T^2}{2} \right]$_{200}^{300} = $\frac{k}{2}$ [$300^2 - 200^2$] = $\frac{k}{2}$ [90000 - 40000] = $\frac{k}{2}$ [50000] = 25000k Given that the heat required is $nk$: Q = nk Comparing with our calculated value: nk = 25000k $\Rightarrow$ n = 25000

questions.question: A liquid at 30°C is poured very slowly into a Calorimeter that is at temperature of 110°C. The boiling temperature of the liquid is 80°C. It is found that the first 5 gm of the liquid completely evaporates. After pouring another 80 gm of the liquid the equilibrium temperature is found to be 50°C. The ratio of the Latent heat of the liquid to its specific heat will be ______ °C. [Neglect the heat exchange with surrounding]
questions.explanation: Let m = mass of calorimeter, x = specific heat of calorimeter s = specific heat of liquid L = latent heat of liquid First 5 g of liquid at 30° is poured to calorimeter at 110°C ∴ $m \times x \times (110 - 80) = 5 \times s \times (80 - 30) + 5 L \Rightarrow mx \times 30 = 250 s + 5 L \dots (i)$ Now, 80 g of liquid at 30° is poured into calorimeter at 80°C, the equilibrium temperature reaches to 50°C. ∴ $m \times x \times (80 - 50) = 80 \times s \times (50 - 30) \Rightarrow mx \times 30 = 1600 s \dots (ii)$ From (i) & (ii) $250 s + 5 L = 1600 s \Rightarrow 5L = 1350 s \Rightarrow \frac{L}{s} = 270$
